prompt.context: Our client, GGC Health, operates eight Ambulatory Surgical Centers (ASC) on the east coast. GGC Health has consistently been a profitable organization, but over the past two years, their ASCs' cumulative revenues have been flat at $400 million/year. The CEO of GGC Health is concerned about this and has hired your firm to increase revenues by 15%.
prompt.question: How would you help GGC Health increase its revenues by 15%?

clarifying_info.a: ASCs are modern health care facilities focused on providing same-day surgical care, including diagnostic and preventive procedures. They are seen as a more convenient alternative to hospital-based outpatient procedures.

clarifying_info.q: Who decides where a surgery is performed?
clarifying_info.a: Physicians generally dictate where the surgery is performed. They can perform surgeries at hospitals or ASCs.
No, pricing increases are not possible.

clarifying_info.q: What is GGC Health's revenue model?
clarifying_info.a: ASC revenue equals the number of procedures performed in the facility multiplied by the expected reimbursement per procedure.

exhibits.title: Physician Group Membership by City
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing the percentage breakdown of physician specialties (Orthopedic, Neurology, Gastroenterology) across three candidate expansion cities: Charlotte, Indianapolis, and Nashville.
exhibits.data: Charlotte: Orthopedic 80%, Neurology 10%, Gastroenterology 10%. Indianapolis: Orthopedic 40%, Neurology 40%, Gastroenterology 20%. Nashville: Orthopedic 50%, Neurology 25%, Gastroenterology 25%.

exhibits.title: Average Reimbursement Rates Per Patient by Specialty
exhibits.shows: A table listing reimbursement rates per patient for six physician specialties.
exhibits.data: Dermatology $4,000; Gastroenterology $15,000; Neurology $25,000; Orthopedic $5,000; Pain Management $6,000; Urology $8,000.

framework: Increase revenue at existing 8 ASCs: grow number of patients per doctor, grow number of doctors per facility, shift product mix toward higher-reimbursement procedures, expand payer mix toward higher-reimbursement patients

Increase revenue by opening new ASCs: analyze market demand and patient demographics, evaluate physician group partnerships, assess competitor landscape (other ASCs, hospital strength), consider regulatory and reimbursement environment (fee-for-service vs. value-based care)

questions.prompt: GGC Health has identified three potential expansion cities: Charlotte (30 doctors), Indianapolis (25 doctors), and Nashville (16 doctors). Given management can open only one new ASC immediately, which city should they enter?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 to calculate the number of doctors per specialty in each city (total doctors × specialty percentage). An excellent candidate will quickly eliminate Nashville because Indianapolis has more doctors in every specialty than Nashville. Charlotte vs. Indianapolis then requires a revenue calculation (Question 2).

math.setup: Multiply total doctors per city by the specialty percentage from Exhibit 1 to get doctors per specialty per city.
steps: Nashville eliminated: Indianapolis exceeds Nashville in every specialty (10>8, 10>4, 5>4)
math.answer: Nashville is eliminated. The decision is between Charlotte and Indianapolis, requiring revenue analysis.

questions.prompt: Calculate the projected annual revenue for Charlotte and Indianapolis to determine which city to recommend.
questions.guidance: Patients per doctor per month: Ortho 15, Neuro 10, Gastro 12. Candidate must ask for reimbursement rates; provide Exhibit 2. Calculate patients/year per doctor, then revenue per doctor per year, then multiply by doctor count per specialty per city and sum. Candidate should identify Indianapolis as the most attractive option at ~$49.8M, but note this alone falls short of the $60M target (15% of $400M).

math.setup: Revenue per doctor per year = (patients/doctor/month × 12 months) × reimbursement rate. Total city revenue = sum over specialties of (doctors per specialty × revenue per doctor per year).
steps: Patients/year per doctor: Ortho 15×12=180; Neuro 10×12=120; Gastro 12×12=144
Charlotte revenue: Ortho 24×$900K=$21.6M; Neuro 3×$3M=$9M; Gastro 3×$2.16M=$6.48M → Total $37.08M
Indianapolis revenue: Ortho 10×$900K=$9M; Neuro 10×$3M=$30M; Gastro 5×$2.16M=$10.8M → Total $49.8M
Nashville revenue (for reference): Ortho 8×$900K=$7.2M; Neuro 4×$3M=$12M; Gastro 4×$2.16M=$8.64M → Total $27.84M
Revenue gap: $60M target − $49.8M (Indianapolis) = $10.2M still needed from existing sites
math.answer: Indianapolis generates ~$49.8M in projected annual revenue vs. Charlotte's $37.08M. Indianapolis is the preferred city, but it alone does not meet the $60M target, so additional same-site revenue growth is required.

questions.prompt: Indianapolis alone does not reach the $60M revenue target. How could GGC Health increase revenues at its current 8 ASC locations to close the gap?
questions.guidance: This is a structured brainstorm. Candidate should organize ideas into buckets: (1) Increase patients per doctor — make ASC the preferred venue by offering scheduling control, efficiency, better patient outcomes, profit-sharing incentives, prioritize high-volume doctors; (2) Increase doctors per ASC — recruit new physicians, new procedure lines, outreach/marketing; (3) Improve product mix — prioritize high-reimbursement surgeries, add new high-reimbursement specialties, consider payer mix (Medicaid/Medicare vs. private insurance).

questions.prompt: GGC Health can add 2 urology doctors to each of the current 8 ASC sites. Each urologist brings in 8 patients per doctor per month. Calculate the additional revenue this would generate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize Exhibit 2 already contains the urology reimbursement rate ($8,000). Total urologists = 8 sites × 2 = 16. Total patients per year = 16 × (8 × 12) = 1,536, rounded to 1,500. Revenue = 1,500 × $8,000 = $12M. This combined with Indianapolis ($49.8M) meets and slightly exceeds the $60M target ($49.8M + $12M = $61.8M).

math.setup: Total urologists across all sites × annual patients per urologist × reimbursement rate per patient.
steps: Patients per urologist per year: 8 patients/month × 12 months = 96 patients/year
Combined new revenue: $49.8M (Indianapolis) + $12M (urology) = $61.8M, exceeding the $60M target
math.answer: Adding urology generates $12M in additional revenue. Combined with the Indianapolis ASC ($49.8M), total incremental revenue is ~$61.8M, exceeding the $60M (15%) target.

brainstorming.prompt: How could GGC Health increase revenues at its current 8 ASC locations?

categories.name: Increase patients per doctor
ideas: Make ASC the preferred venue for physicians by offering more control over the environment and scheduling
Improve efficiency and patient outcomes to attract high-volume doctors
Provide physicians with a higher profit share for hitting patient volume targets
Prioritize recruiting and retaining high-volume doctors

categories.name: Increase doctors per ASC
ideas: Add physicians in new procedure lines (e.g., urology as shown in Q4)
Conduct improved physician outreach and marketing to recruit new doctors
Partner with physician groups to bring in additional specialists

categories.name: Improve product and payer mix
ideas: Prioritize high-reimbursement surgeries (neurology, gastroenterology over orthopedic)
Add new high-reimbursement specialties not currently offered
Review payer mix: increase share of patients with higher reimbursement insurance plans
Evaluate whether to accept or expand Medicaid/Medicare and weigh reimbursement implications

recommendation: Open a new ASC in Indianapolis, projected to generate ~$49.8M in additional annual revenue
Add 2 urology doctors to each of the 8 existing ASC sites, generating ~$12M in additional annual revenue
Together these two initiatives deliver ~$61.8M in incremental revenue, exceeding the 15% ($60M) target
risks: No cost analysis was performed for the new Indianapolis facility or the urology expansion — profitability is unconfirmed
Indianapolis is not on the east coast, putting it outside management's geographic familiarity
ASC capacity at existing sites may need to expand to accommodate new urology procedures
Actual physician volume may fall short of projections if doctors do not bring in the expected number of patients
Market share assumptions for Indianapolis may not materialize if competitor ASCs or hospital outpatient departments are strong
next_steps: Conduct a full cost-benefit analysis for the Indianapolis location before committing to construction
If still attractive, begin site selection and construction on the Indianapolis ASC
Add urology to current ASC sites immediately as a lower-risk, faster-return initiative
Evaluate additional new specialty lines (e.g., dermatology, pain management) for existing sites
Consider a longer-term pipeline of new ASC locations beyond Indianapolis
